content: 1. Recommendations for data evaluation should focus on ensuring that the most relevant items to the project are assessed. These recommendations will be shaped by the Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) team’s expertise in the subject matter. 2. For data collection, it is essential to determine whether the data elements for each indicator are clearly defined. If they are not, specific changes should be recommended to address this issue. 3. It is important to assess whether there are automated or manual validation checks for the data elements in the dataset. If such checks are absent, recommendations should be made to improve the quality assurance processes. 4. The feasibility of linking relevant databases to support the project’s or program’s claims should be evaluated. This includes identifying which databases should be linked and determining the appropriate identifiers to facilitate this linkage. 5. If data from paper forms are required to support the claims, the accessibility of this data and the existence of a system linking paper data to digital data should be assessed. If such a system is not in place, recommendations should be made to enhance data use and accessibility. 6. The adequacy of the system for data backup, archiving, and updating should be evaluated to ensure proper data storage. 7. Data security measures should be reviewed to confirm that they are adequate and meet the necessary standards. 8. The usability of data dashboards should be assessed. This includes determining whether the data can be conveniently exported into a usable format and shared, and whether the level of disaggregation and reporting for each indicator aligns with how the indicator should be measured. If not, changes should be recommended. 9. The intuitiveness of the dashboard and its usage by leadership for reporting purposes should be evaluated. 10. The adequacy of staff support for the project, given its size, should be assessed. Additionally, the sufficiency of training time provided, considering the project’s complexity, should be reviewed. 11. If a supervisory role exists, the level of supervision should be evaluated to determine whether it is adequate for the scale of the operation. 12. Documentation for key program operations and procedures should be reviewed. Areas that would benefit from improved documentation should be identified. 13. Regular meetings to discuss data management and use should be held. The inclusion of data quality discussions in these meetings, based on existing meeting records, should be confirmed. 14. The relevance of research findings should be assessed to determine their potential for replication in effective digital health interventions. Clear and comprehensive information, including evaluation methodology and the use of specific technologies and platforms, should be provided. 15. The mHealth Evidence Reporting and Assessment (mERA) checklist was developed to address the lack of systematic and useful reporting for digital health interventions and associated research studies. It aims to promote clarity and completeness in reporting research involving mobile tools in healthcare. 16. The mERA checklist provides guidance for transparent and complete reporting on studies evaluating the feasibility and effectiveness of digital health interventions. It is not intended to support the design or implementation of such studies but rather to improve transparency and rigor in reporting research findings. 17. The checklist is designed for use by authors developing manuscripts on the effectiveness of digital health interventions and by peer reviewers and journal editors reviewing such evidence. It should also be reviewed before starting any M&E activity planned for publication to ensure necessary reporting criteria are met. 18. The mERA checklist includes 16 core criteria and an additional 29 items for reporting on study design and methods. These criteria were developed to guide methodological reporting of digital health evidence, particularly for exploratory study designs. 19. Authors should describe the minimum enabling infrastructure required for program implementation, including physical infrastructure such as electricity, power access, and connectivity in the local context. This information is critical for understanding the feasibility, generalizability, and replicability of digital health innovations in other settings. 20. The choice of software and hardware used in the deployment of the digital health intervention should be clearly explained. This includes describing any modifications made to publicly available software. Such information is essential for contextualizing the authors’ work and comparing it to other innovations. 21. The potential for integration of the digital health strategy into existing health information systems (HIS) should be described, regardless of whether such integration has been achieved. 22. The delivery of the digital health intervention, including the mode of delivery (e.g., SMS, face-to-face, interactive voice response), timing, and duration, should be detailed. 23. The content of the intervention, including its source and any modifications, should be described. 24. Formative research, content testing, and usability testing with the target group(s) should be clearly identified and described. 25. User feedback on the intervention, including user satisfaction, opinions on content or user interface, and perceptions of usability, access, and connectivity, should be reported. 26. Barriers or facilitators to the adoption of the intervention among study participants should be mentioned. This includes individual-level structural, economic, and social factors that may limit a user’s ability to adopt the intervention. 27. Basic cost assessments of the digital health intervention from various perspectives should be presented. If a formal economic evaluation has been conducted, it should be mentioned with appropriate references. 28. The mechanisms used to inform people about the program, including training and promotional activities, should be described. 29. Limitations of the digital health intervention for delivery at scale should be clearly presented. 30. The adaptability of the solution to different languages, populations, or contexts should be described, including any modifications resulting from pilot testing or usability assessments. 31. Details supporting the replicability of the intervention, such as source code, screenshots, flowcharts, or examples of messages, should be provided. 32. Data security procedures and confidentiality protocols should be described. 33. Compliance with national guidelines or regulatory statutes should be detailed, including mechanisms to ensure alignment with existing standards. 34. Authors should strive to describe the minimum infrastructure required for program implementation to facilitate understanding of the feasibility and replicability of the digital health innovation in other contexts.
